t: The Marinids took Fez in 1248 and Marrakesh in 1269, ending Almohad rule in the western Maghreb; in 1276 they founded Fes Jdid as their administrative and military centre.

Abu al-Hasan (r. 1331–1348) conquered Tlemcen in 1337 and defeated the Hafsids in 1347, making himself master of a territory from southern Morocco to Tripoli, but lost his eastern lands within a year.
A Portuguese–Castilian army defeated the Marinids at the Battle of Río Salado in 1340 and Castile took Algeciras in 1344, expelling them from the Iberian Peninsula for good.
dyk: Abu al-Hasan copied the Qur'an in his own hand four times, sending copies to Medina, Mecca and the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem; a fifth, begun at Bijaya for Hebron, was finished by his son after his dethronement.
ev: Abu Yahya's reign begins; between 1244 and 1248 the Marinids take Taza, Rabat, Salé, Meknes and Fez from the weakened Almohads.
Abu Yusuf Yaqub captures Marrakesh, effectively ending Almohad rule.
Fes Jdid, 'New Fez', is founded as the dynasty's administrative and military centre.
The Marinids hold Rota, Tarifa and Gibraltar, seeking control of the Strait's trade from Algeciras.
Abu al-Hasan conquers the Abdalwadid kingdom of Tlemcen.
A Portuguese–Castilian army defeats the Marinids at the Battle of Río Salado near Tarifa.
Abu al-Hasan defeats the Hafsids of Ifriqiya and rules from southern Morocco to Tripoli; within a year a revolt of Arab tribes in southern Tunisia costs him the east.
Abd al-Haqq II, the last Marinid sultan, is killed in a revolt in Fez after appointing a Jewish vizier, Aaron ben Batash.

f.capital: Fez (Fes Jdid, the new city founded in 1276); Taza for the early emirs
f.founder: Abd al-Haqq I, the effective founder; the dynasty is named for its ancestor Marin ibn Wartajan al-Zenati
f.predecessor: The Almohad Caliphate, whose capital Marrakesh fell to the Marinids in 1269
f.successor: The Wattasid dynasty, regents from 1420 and sultans in Fez from 1472; the Hintata of Marrakesh; Portugal and Castile on the coast
